prize_parts.citation: for discoveries establishing GLP-1 as an incretin hormone and defining its active form and actions, enabling incretin-based therapies for diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six of us placed B012 first, but that agreement is not the argument. The argument is that the discovery chain is unusually complete: proglucagon processing and the identification of the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, the human physiology of the incretin effect, and the demonstration that the hormone's actions can be exploited pharmacologically. It has been confirmed in large independent randomized outcome trials, and it changed practice in two fields, diabetes and obesity, with cardiovascular and renal benefit now documented. It is mature rather than premature. A single-achievement prize naming Drucker, Holst and Mojsov honours the physiology and peptide biology that made the drugs possible without forcing an arbitrary split with a second discovery.
statement.case_against: The three-laureate ceiling excludes Lotte Bjerre Knudsen, whose liraglutide and semaglutide engineering is what made GLP-1 a medicine, and the supplied credit list omits other early contributors such as Habener. Mojsov's priority for the active peptide is contested in the record, and I cannot verify the details independently. If the committee thinks the prize should reward the therapeutic achievement and not the physiology, my trio is the wrong one, and the case for Knudsen becomes strong. B012 is also so dominant that it risks crowding out discoveries with comparable conceptual depth, such as the unfolded protein response, which I regard as the strongest purely mechanistic case on the list.

responses.point: Thomas proposed the three basic-science names for B012 and left out Knudsen, noting that the Mojsov priority is contested and Habener is absent from the list.
responses.response: I agree on the trio, with the same reservation about Mojsov. Excluding Knudsen is defensible on the grounds that the Nobel tradition rewards the discovery of the mechanism over its pharmaceutical optimisation, and the physiology was in place before any long-acting agonist existed. But I would not call her contribution merely industrial. Making a peptide with a half-life of days, with demonstrated efficacy, was a scientific achievement, and if Mojsov's priority proves weaker than the record suggests, I would reopen the question of whether Knudsen should take her place. I would not widen the prize to a fourth name.

responses.point: Per ranked BCR-ABL inhibition (B016) second, as a paradigm of rationally targeted therapy with exceptional clarity from compound to patient and two decades of survival data.
responses.response: I accept that B016 is mature and that its clinical impact is exceptional. My difficulty is the framing. The prize would honour a drug, and the oncogene biology that made the target rational lies outside this entry's credited names, so the citation would credit the translation and leave out the discovery that justified it. B012 has the same chemist-clinician tension but does include the underlying physiology among its credited names. I rank B016 below the UPR and CAR-T cases for this reason, and I am willing to be persuaded if you can show that the credited trio is the right cut of the targeted-therapy story.

responses.point: Marie ranked TNF blockade (B046) second, arguing a clean two-person configuration in Feldmann and Maini and a bedside-to-bench logic that established anti-cytokine therapy across several diseases.
responses.response: The two-person attribution is cleaner than most on our list and the clinical durability is not in doubt. My reservation is whether it is basic enough: the mechanistic insight that TNF drives synovial inflammation was important, but the field-changing step was largely the drug class, and I would want to understand how much the antibody engineering and industrial developers' work is being set aside. I see it as a respectable second-tier candidate rather than a leading one, but I would take it seriously as one of the two parts of a shared prize if the committee prefers a medicine-focused pairing with B012.

responses.point: Sten placed B009 (CAR-T) second with June, Sadelain and Rosenberg as a plausible trio, noting that Eshhar's original chimeric-receptor concept is not in the credited names.
responses.response: I take the Eshhar issue as more than a footnote. The concept of a chimeric T-cell receptor is the originality, and the costimulated clinical versions are the realisation, so a prize crediting only the latter would be vulnerable. I also doubt Rosenberg belongs on a CAR-T citation, as his adoptive-transfer work is distinct and arguably deserves recognition in its own right. That is why I put B009 fourth and not second: I think it is a strong candidate, but the attribution problem needs resolving before it can be put on the same footing as B012 or B024. I disagree with the framing that it is the natural second part of a shared prize.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's contribution to identifying the active GLP-1 peptide is adequately established relative to Habener and colleagues, who are not on the credited list.
Whether the committee wants to honour physiology and peptide biology or the drug-development achievement, and whether Knudsen should replace one of the three names.
Whether B024 (Walter and Mori) should be paired with B012 in a shared prize, given that the three-person limit cannot accommodate both in full.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B012. I have co-authored with Sten Linnarsson and Jonas Frisen and share an institution with several colleagues, but none of the credited candidates for B012 appears in my documented record, and I would disclose any connection that emerged for other candidates.
